question_en: I want to start tourism but I think my village has nothing special. How do I find what visitors would like?
answer: Visitors often enjoy ordinary daily life that locals take for granted. Walk through a normal day and a normal year in your village and list everything people do, make, grow, cook, sing or celebrate. Ask elders, women and youth separately, because each group notices different things.
actions: Draw a simple list with headings: farm, kitchen, craft, music, festivals, water, walks, stories, buildings, work, seasons.
Ask five people of different ages to add to the list without judging any item.
Mark each item with who owns the skill or place, so you know whose permission is needed.
caution: Do not list sacred places, private family rituals or sensitive items for visitors until the owners agree.
evidence: Kerala RT native experiences page (read) shows ordinary work such as fishing, farming, weaving, cooking as visitor experiences; method is general practice.

question_en: I have ten ideas for visitors. How do I decide which ones are worth doing?
answer: Test each idea against six questions: Is it real (authentic)? Is it safe? Does the community welcome it? Can a visitor understand it in their language? Can you repeat it many times without tiring the host? Is it low-impact on water, waste and quiet? Keep only ideas that pass all six.
actions: Write the six questions on a sheet and score each idea yes, maybe or no.
Drop ideas with any 'no' on safety or community welcome.
Pilot the two or three best ideas first.
caution: Safety and community consent are not negotiable. A 'maybe' on these means stop and ask more people.
evidence: Good practice for village hosts; consistent with community-tourism principles in the bank sources, no single rule.

question_en: How do I name my activity so guests understand it and want to book?
answer: Use a simple name that says what the guest does, plus a place or person. Example only: 'Make rotis on a chulha with Sunita-ji'. Avoid big words like 'ultimate' or 'authentic'. Say what the guest will actually do in clear words.
actions: Write the name in plain words with a verb such as cook, weave, walk or plant.
Add the village name and the season if it matters.
Read the name aloud to a guest and ask if the activity is clear.
caution: Do not use a deity, tribe or sacred name as a brand without community permission.
evidence: Good practice for village hosts; consistent with community-tourism principles in the bank sources, no single rule.

question_en: What is a 'visitor promise' and how do I write one that I can keep?
answer: A visitor promise is one sentence saying what the guest will see, learn or do and how long it takes. Write only what you can deliver on a bad day too. Example only: 'In two hours you will learn to make three village dishes and eat them with the family.'
actions: Write one sentence with who, what and how long.
Remove any word you cannot guarantee, such as 'best' or 'wildlife sighting'.
Check the promise with the people who will deliver it.
caution: Do not promise nature sightings, weather or festivals. These are not in your control.
evidence: Good practice for village hosts; consistent with community-tourism principles in the bank sources, no single rule.

question_en: I want to tell the story of our village but I do not know the real history. What should I do?
answer: Do not invent history. Sit with elders and ask open questions, then tell the story in their words and name them as the source. If people disagree, say 'some people say...'. Tell guests when something is a belief or tradition and not a proven fact.
actions: Ask elders: Who built this? What did your grandparents do here? What changed in your lifetime?
Record or note their answers only with their permission and tell them how you will use them.
Read the final story back to them for approval before telling guests.
caution: Some stories belong to a family, caste group or temple and may not be for outsiders. Ask first.
evidence: UN Tourism Global Code of Ethics (read) says tourism should let traditional culture survive and not degrade it; method is general practice.

question_en: How do I plan a simple 2-hour experience for guests who come for a short visit?
answer: Keep it to one clear activity with a welcome and a close. A simple shape is: welcome drink (10 min), short talk (10), hands-on activity (60), sharing food or tea (30), thanks and photo with consent (10). Test the timing with friends before selling it.
actions: Write the timed steps on one page.
Prepare materials and seats before guests arrive.
Keep 10 spare minutes for late arrival and questions.
caution: Keep group size small enough for everyone to see and be safe near fire, tools or water.
evidence: Good practice for village hosts; consistent with community-tourism principles in the bank sources, no single rule.

question_en: How do I stretch one activity into a half-day or full-day plan without exhausting my family?
answer: Mix active and rest parts. A half-day can pair one hands-on activity with a short village walk and a meal. A full-day adds a second activity at a different home, so work is shared. Allow rest, toilet breaks and a buffer for delays.
actions: Pair each hands-on activity with a rest or meal.
Involve a second household for the second activity so one family does not carry everything.
Add a short, free-time slot for guests to rest or explore alone.
caution: Long walks and heat need water, shade and a plan for tired guests. Check guest fitness before booking.
evidence: Good practice for village hosts; consistent with community-tourism principles in the bank sources, no single rule.

question_en: How do I design a 2-night stay that does not feel repetitive?
answer: Give each day a different theme and leave empty time. For example: Day 1 arrival, family dinner and a light evening walk; Day 2 farm or craft activity and a village meal; Day 3 slow breakfast and farewell. Do not fill every hour.
actions: Pick one main activity per day.
Leave an afternoon free for rest.
Plan a rain-day version of each activity.
caution: Keep the family dinner and sleeping areas private from public programmes.
evidence: Good practice for village hosts; consistent with community-tourism principles in the bank sources, no single rule.

question_en: What is a good way to welcome and say goodbye to guests that is real to our culture?
answer: Use a small greeting that you already do for guests, such as a drink, a flower, a tilak or tea. Explain it in a sentence so guests understand and can say no politely. A short goodbye with a thank-you and a request for feedback builds trust.
actions: Pick one greeting that is natural for your family.
Tell guests what the ritual means and that taking part is optional.
Say thanks at departure and ask how the guest felt.
caution: Do not stage religious rituals for show. Ask the community or priest what may be shared.
evidence: UN Tourism Global Code of Ethics (read) says tourists must respect local traditions; method is general practice.

question_en: How many guests can I take at one time for a cooking or farm activity?
answer: Set a limit based on your space, safety and how many hosts you have, not on how many bookings you want. A usual rule of thumb is one host for every small group so each guest gets attention. Test your limit in a pilot.
actions: Count seats, tools, toilets and hosts, and take the lowest number as the limit.
Write the limit on your booking message.
Learn to say 'we are full for that time' politely.
caution: Fire, water, animals and tools need closer supervision with bigger groups.
evidence: Good practice for village hosts; consistent with community-tourism principles in the bank sources, no single rule.

question_en: Can I include children, elders and guests who walk slowly in my experience?
answer: Yes, if you ask in advance and change the plan. Offer seats, shade, shorter routes and a slower pace. Keep a lighter version of each activity. Give children tasks that are safe and age-fitting, and keep an adult responsible for them.
actions: Ask guests at booking about age, mobility and health needs.
Prepare a short, flat, shaded version of any walk.
Keep fire, sharp tools and deep water out of children's reach.
caution: Do not give medical advice. For serious conditions, advise the guest to consult their own doctor before booking.
evidence: Good practice for village hosts; consistent with community-tourism principles in the bank sources, no single rule.

question_en: What do I do with guests when it rains or is very hot or cold?
answer: Plan an indoor or covered version of every outdoor activity before you sell it. Tell guests at booking what changes in rain, heat or cold. If conditions are unsafe, change or stop the activity and refund or reschedule fairly.
actions: Write a rain plan and a heat plan for each activity.
Keep umbrellas, raincoats, drinking water and shade ready.
Decide in advance who calls it off and by what time.
caution: Lightning, floods, landslides and extreme heat are real dangers. Follow local authority warnings.
evidence: Good practice for village hosts; consistent with community-tourism principles in the bank sources, no single rule.
verify_with: District disaster management / local weather advisory

question_en: How do I work out what to charge for my experience? I only guess now.
answer: List every cost of one session: food, materials, fuel, your time, helpers' pay, cleaning, wear on tools, a community share, and a small saving for repairs. Add them, divide by the number of guests, then compare with what similar experiences charge. Do this before you quote any price.
actions: Write each cost on a page for one full session.
Add a line for your own time and for a rest-day reserve.
Divide the total by the guests you realistically get, not the maximum.
caution: Example only, use your own numbers: if the total cost of a session is 2,000 and 10 guests come, the cost per guest is 200 before any profit.
evidence: Good practice for village hosts; consistent with community-tourism principles in the bank sources, no single rule. For tax and licence questions, ask a qualified accountant or the relevant authority.

question_en: How do I decide how much to pay the cook, guide, musician or elder who helps with a visit?
answer: Pay everyone who gives time or skill, in cash and on time, even family members. Agree the amount before the visit, in front of the group. Pay for skill and preparation time too, not only for the hour on stage. Keep a simple note of who was paid what.
actions: Ask each person what they consider fair before the first pilot.
Write the agreed pay in a notebook and read it out.
Pay on the day or on an agreed date and keep a record.
caution: Do not expect elders or women to give their skill free because it is 'culture'. Culture is livelihood here.
evidence: UN Tourism Global Code of Ethics (read) says local people should share equitably in benefits; method is general practice.

question_en: Should we collect a small amount from every guest for the village? How does it work?
answer: Some community tourism groups add a small, fixed share to every booking for a village fund. Decide the share in a meeting, write it down, and show guests where it is spent. Keep it separate from the family's income and report it openly.
actions: Agree in a public meeting what the share is and what it is for.
Keep the money in a separate account or box with two keepers.
Read out the income and spending every few months.
caution: Rules on accounts, receipts and tax apply. Ask your gram panchayat, a bank or a chartered accountant how to hold community money safely.
evidence: General practice, consistent with benefit-sharing in UN Tourism Global Code of Ethics (read).

question_en: Can I charge more in season and less in off-season? Will guests mind?
answer: Yes. Many hosts charge more when demand is high and less when it is slow. Fix the dates in advance and keep them on the same page as your booking message. Do not change prices after a guest has been quoted.
actions: Mark your high, normal and slow months on a calendar.
Publish the rate for each season in one clear table.
Honour the price quoted when the guest booked.
caution: Festival dates move each year. Check the calendar before you promise a rate.
evidence: Good practice for village hosts; consistent with community-tourism principles in the bank sources, no single rule.

question_en: Should I charge per person or one price for the whole package?
answer: Per-person pricing is simple for mixed groups. A package price covering stay, meals and activity is easier for families and avoids small arguments. State clearly what is included and what is extra, such as drinks, transport or tips.
actions: Write 'included' and 'extra' as two short lists.
Offer a family or group package if your costs do not rise by guest.
Tell guests the total before arrival.
evidence: Good practice for village hosts; consistent with community-tourism principles in the bank sources, no single rule.

question_en: Guests say my price is too low and I still earn little. Am I underpricing?
answer: You may be. Many new hosts count only food and forget their time, cleaning, repairs and slow months. If you are tired and the money is thin, your price is likely too low. Re-do your cost sheet and add the missing items.
actions: Add your own and family labour hours to the cost sheet.
Include a reserve for slow months and repairs.
Raise the price slowly and watch if bookings stay.
caution: Do not copy a far cheaper neighbour. Their costs and quality may be different.
evidence: Good practice for village hosts; consistent with community-tourism principles in the bank sources, no single rule.

question_en: A guest says 'why is this so costly for a village?' How do I explain?
answer: Be calm and show where the money goes. Say that the price pays the cook, the guide, the family, the food and a share to the village. Give a short, honest breakdown. Do not argue and do not drop the price just to avoid awkwardness.
actions: Prepare a three-line price explanation.
Show who benefits from each part, with no private details.
Offer a smaller option if the guest cannot afford the full one.
evidence: Good practice for village hosts; consistent with community-tourism principles in the bank sources, no single rule.

question_en: Should I ask for advance money? How do I handle it if guests cancel?
answer: Yes, a small advance protects you from no-shows. Write the advance amount and the refund rule before booking, in the same message as the price. Give a written or WhatsApp receipt for every payment.
actions: Write the advance and refund rule in two simple lines.
Send a receipt message on every payment.
Refund fairly when you cancel because of weather or illness.
caution: Consumer, GST and payment rules apply. For tax and licence questions, ask a qualified accountant or the relevant authority.
evidence: Good practice for village hosts; consistent with community-tourism principles in the bank sources, no single rule.

question_en: How do I write a fair cancellation policy in simple words?
answer: Use simple steps by time: more days before arrival means a bigger refund, last-minute means less. Add one line for weather or safety cancellation by you. Show the policy before the guest pays.
actions: Draft three time slabs with refund shares written in words.
State what happens if you must cancel.
Keep a screenshot of the guest's agreement.
caution: Do not copy a rule you cannot follow. Fair and consistent matters more than strict.
evidence: Good practice for village hosts; consistent with community-tourism principles in the bank sources, no single rule.
verify_with: Local lawyer or tourism department if disputes

question_en: Big groups ask for discount. How much should I give, and when?
answer: Give a discount only if your cost per guest really falls, for example, a shared meal or one guide for more guests. Do not cut below your cost sheet. Offer a fixed group rate in writing instead of case-by-case bargaining.
actions: Check your cost sheet for savings at larger group sizes.
Set one group rate and publish it.
Say no politely if the offered rate loses money.
evidence: Good practice for village hosts; consistent with community-tourism principles in the bank sources, no single rule.

question_en: Should I give receipts to guests? What should I write?
answer: A simple receipt builds trust. Write the date, guest name, what was paid for, the amount and how it was paid, then sign. Keep a copy in a notebook. Ask an accountant whether you need a formal bill or tax invoice.
actions: Use a numbered receipt book or a standard message in WhatsApp.
Keep a copy of each receipt in order.
Ask an accountant if you need a formal invoice.
caution: Tax and invoice rules are covered by other guidance. Ask a qualified accountant.
evidence: Good practice for village hosts; consistent with community-tourism principles in the bank sources, no single rule.

question_en: How do I write a description that sells but is honest?
answer: Say what guests will do, who will host them, how long it takes, what is included, and what is simple or basic. Name limits, such as no AC, hand pump water or a short walk from the road. Honesty reduces complaints and bad reviews.
actions: Write a short description with what, who, how long and what is included.
List two basic things guests should expect, such as squat toilet or power cuts.
Show photos of the real room and the real kitchen.
caution: Words like 'authentic' or 'untouched' can over-promise. Describe what you do instead.
evidence: Good practice for village hosts; consistent with community-tourism principles in the bank sources, no single rule.

question_en: Can I put photos of my guests, children or neighbours on Instagram and WhatsApp?
answer: Ask first, every time. Take a person's photo or video for promotion only after they say yes, and tell them where it will appear. Do not post photos of children or of guests without clear permission from them or their parent.
actions: Ask 'May I take your photo for our page?' and wait for yes.
Keep a simple note or message showing who agreed.
Delete a photo promptly if someone asks.
caution: Privacy law on personal data is changing. Ask a legal or data authority for the current rules before keeping or sharing photos and guest details.
evidence: UN Tourism Global Code of Ethics (read) calls for respect for people; consent practice is general.
verify_with: Legal adviser on data and privacy rules

question_en: How can I take good photos for my homestay with only a mobile phone?
answer: Clean the space, use daylight and hold the phone steady. Take a wide shot of each room, the bed, the toilet, the view, the kitchen and one activity in use. Avoid heavy filters. Photos must look like what guests will really find.
actions: Clean and tidy each room, then take photos in morning daylight.
Shoot landscape-style wide photos and keep the phone level.
Take photos of real people at work, with consent.
caution: Do not use photos from the internet or other places.
evidence: Good practice for village hosts; consistent with community-tourism principles in the bank sources, no single rule.

question_en: Should I make short videos? What can I show?
answer: A 20 to 40 second video of a real activity is helpful. Show the welcome, the activity, the food and the host speaking. Keep sound clear and ask everyone in the frame for permission. Do not film sacred events or private spaces.
actions: Film a short, steady clip of one real activity.
Add a caption saying what, where and how to book.
Get permission from everyone who appears.
caution: Rituals, funerals, prayers and children's bathing or changing must never be filmed.
evidence: Good practice for village hosts; consistent with community-tourism principles in the bank sources, no single rule.

question_en: Guests message on WhatsApp all day. How do I reply properly without losing my time?
answer: Prepare three saved replies: a greeting with price and what is included, a booking confirmation, and a pre-arrival message. Reply within a day and say your usual reply hours. A short, polite and clear reply is better than a long one.
actions: Save a greeting, a price message and a confirmation as templates.
Tell guests your reply hours.
Ask for dates, group size, diet and phone number in the first reply.
caution: Do not share guests' numbers or ID details in groups.
evidence: Good practice for village hosts; consistent with community-tourism principles in the bank sources, no single rule.

question_en: Guests ask the same questions again and again. Can I make one sheet?
answer: Yes. Write answers to the ten most common questions: how to reach, what to carry, food, toilet type, hot water, charging, network, safety, price and cancellation. Send it after booking and keep a printed copy for check-in.
actions: List the ten questions guests ask you most often.
Write each answer in two lines.
Send the sheet by WhatsApp after the booking.
evidence: Good practice for village hosts; consistent with community-tourism principles in the bank sources, no single rule.

question_en: How do I get reviews from guests without begging?
answer: Ask at departure when the guest is happy. Share the link or QR code and say that honest feedback helps you improve. Never pay for reviews or write fake ones. Thank guests who review.
actions: Ask for feedback at farewell.
Share the review link and a short thank-you message.
Read every review and note what to fix.
caution: Fake or paid reviews can break platform rules and the law. Avoid them.
evidence: Good practice for village hosts; consistent with community-tourism principles in the bank sources, no single rule.

question_en: A guest gave a bad review. What do I do?
answer: Wait a day and read it calmly. Reply politely, thank the guest, say what you will check, and avoid arguing or blaming. If the review is wrong, state the facts briefly. Fix any real problem and tell the next guests about the change.
actions: Wait before replying, then write two calm lines.
Check whether the complaint is true and fix it.
Never reveal the guest's private details in the reply.
caution: If the review is abusive, report it to the platform.
evidence: Good practice for village hosts; consistent with community-tourism principles in the bank sources, no single rule.

question_en: How do I get more guests without paying heavy commission?
answer: Good service creates repeat guests and referrals. Stay in touch through a thank-you message, a festival greeting and a seasonal update. Ask happy guests to recommend you. A small thank-you for a referral is fine if it is honest and fair.
actions: Save guest numbers only with permission and send a thank-you after departure.
Share a seasonal update once or twice a year.
Offer something small, like a tea or a nicer table, for returning guests.
caution: Do not send many messages. Respect opt-outs.
evidence: Good practice for village hosts; consistent with community-tourism principles in the bank sources, no single rule.

question_en: A blogger and a travel agent both want to work with me. How should I respond?
answer: Ask for details in writing: who they are, what they will do, the dates and the rate or commission. Offer a short, real stay and clear rules on photos. Treat all guests the same way and do not give free stays beyond what you can afford.
actions: Ask for their past work and contact details.
Agree commission, dates and photo rules in writing.
Review the result after the first booking.
caution: Check that agents are genuine. Ask your district tourism office or other hosts about them.
evidence: Good practice for village hosts; consistent with community-tourism principles in the bank sources, no single rule.

question_en: How do I tell our story without making our village look poor or backward?
answer: Show people as skilled, proud and capable. Do not ask guests to feel sorry or to give charity. Avoid staged poverty, begging or showing houses and bodies as spectacle. Tell stories of skills, food, work and nature in your own words.
actions: Describe people by their skills and work.
Avoid captions that suggest pity or rescue.
Let community members review photos and text before posting.
caution: Do not sell visits to people's homes as a 'zoo'. Always get consent.
evidence: UN Tourism Global Code of Ethics (read) calls for respect for communities' dignity; practice general.

question_en: Guests want 'authentic' experience. How do I avoid over-promising?
answer: Be open about what is everyday life and what is arranged for guests. If you cook a special dish for visitors, say so. Do not stage rituals as daily life. Guests respect honesty more than perfection.
actions: Label each activity as 'daily life' or 'arranged for guests'.
Describe how you would normally do it and how you changed it for guests.
Check every claim with the people who do the work.
evidence: Good practice for village hosts; consistent with community-tourism principles in the bank sources, no single rule.

question_en: Visitors come only in a few months. How do I plan for the slow season?
answer: Expect slow months and plan for them. Keep other work, such as farming or crafts, going. Offer seasonal experiences, such as harvest or monsoon walks, and use the slow time for repairs, training and planning.
actions: Mark slow months on a calendar and plan repairs or training there.
List one activity for each season.
Save a part of peak-season income for slow months.
caution: Do not depend only on tourism income in the first years.
evidence: Good practice for village hosts; consistent with community-tourism principles in the bank sources, no single rule.

question_en: What should I know when hosting Indian families with children and elders?
answer: Families often want shared rooms, simple home-style food, safe spaces for children and fixed meal times. Ask about ages, diet and mobility at booking. Show where children can play safely and point out hazards like wells, ponds and stoves.
actions: Ask the family's ages, diet and special needs when they book.
Show the children's safe play area and the places they must not go.
Agree meal times and early tea at check-in.
caution: Never leave children unsupervised near water, fire or animals.
evidence: Good practice for village hosts; consistent with community-tourism principles in the bank sources, no single rule.

question_en: What do young couples and youth groups expect, and how do I handle them?
answer: They often want privacy, clean rooms, a good view, and a relaxed pace. Youth groups may want music, bonfires or late nights. Tell them your quiet hours and rules at booking. Be friendly and clear, and do not feel shy to say no.
actions: Share quiet hours and rules before they arrive.
Offer a few activities that fit their interest.
Keep a safe place for valuables and tell them where it is.
caution: Check local rules on alcohol, bonfires and loud music with your panchayat or police.
evidence: Good practice for village hosts; consistent with community-tourism principles in the bank sources, no single rule.

question_en: A school wants to bring 40 students. Can we manage? What should I ask first?
answer: Only accept if you have enough space, toilets, hosts and safe water. Ask the teacher for the number of students, ages, teachers, diet and supervision plan. Split into small groups across homes if needed, and keep the teacher responsible for students.
actions: Ask for numbers, ages, teachers and the learning goal in writing.
Split students into small groups with one host each.
Confirm safety, medical contacts and parent consent through the school.
caution: Children's safety comes first. Do not allow unsupervised student time near water, roads or animals.
evidence: Good practice for village hosts; consistent with community-tourism principles in the bank sources, no single rule.

question_en: What do I need to change for older guests?
answer: Offer a ground floor room, a seat in the bathroom, good light, a handrail and a slower pace. Ask about food limits and medicines. Keep a first-aid kit and know the nearest clinic. Do not push strenuous activity.
actions: Ask about mobility, diet and health needs before booking.
Keep a ground-floor room and a clear, well-lit path ready.
Know where the nearest doctor or hospital is.
caution: Do not give medical advice.
evidence: Good practice for village hosts; consistent with community-tourism principles in the bank sources, no single rule.

question_en: What do foreign guests expect that Indian guests may not?
answer: They often want clear written information, a price shown beforehand, safe water, a Western-style or clean toilet, a mosquito net and honest answers. They may be new to Indian food, heat and customs. Explain things kindly and gently, without assuming they know.
actions: Send an information sheet in simple English before arrival.
Explain food spice, water and toilet style in advance.
Keep a simple cultural note on dress and etiquette.
caution: Legal rules for foreign guests, such as registration of guest details, must be checked with local authorities.
evidence: Good practice for village hosts; consistent with community-tourism principles in the bank sources, no single rule.

question_en: How do I make a solo woman guest feel safe in my home?
answer: Be clear on privacy and safety. Give a room with a good lock, tell her who is in the house, share a contact number, and arrange safe, known transport. Do not ask personal questions. Female family members should be present where possible.
actions: Check the room lock and light before arrival.
Share a host contact number and arrange safe local transport.
Respect her privacy and ask before sharing her details.
caution: Never share a woman guest's room number or details with unknown callers.
evidence: Good practice for village hosts; consistent with community-tourism principles in the bank sources, no single rule.

question_en: Some guests want to work from my homestay for weeks. What should I tell them?
answer: Be honest about internet speed and power cuts. Offer a quiet table, charging points and a power backup if you have it. Agree a weekly price and meal arrangement, and tell them when the family is busy or noisy.
actions: Test your internet at different times and tell the true speed.
Set up a quiet worktable and a charger point.
Agree long-stay terms, laundry and meals in writing.
caution: Do not promise 'high speed internet' unless tested.
evidence: Good practice for village hosts; consistent with community-tourism principles in the bank sources, no single rule.

question_en: Photographers and bird watchers want early mornings and quiet. How do I manage them?
answer: Offer early tea, a packed breakfast and a local guide who knows the area. Explain rules: stay on paths, keep distance, do not disturb nests, and no playback or drones unless allowed. Ask for photos only with permission when people appear.
actions: Offer an early tea and a packed breakfast.
Tell them the rules for wildlife, nests and distance.
Hire a trained local guide for the best places.
caution: Drone and protected-area rules differ. Ask the forest or local authority.
evidence: Good practice for village hosts; consistent with community-tourism principles in the bank sources, no single rule.

question_en: Pilgrims and very religious guests have food and ritual needs. How do I serve them?
answer: Ask about food rules, fasting, prayer times and bathing needs at booking. Keep a separate cooking area or utensils for strict vegetarian guests where possible. Be honest about what you can offer and do not claim what you cannot do.
actions: Ask about diet and prayer needs at booking.
Offer separate utensils where you can.
Tell guests about nearby temples, mosques or other places respectfully.
caution: Do not promise 'jain', 'halal' or 'pure' food unless you can truly follow the rules.
evidence: Good practice for village hosts; consistent with community-tourism principles in the bank sources, no single rule.

question_en: Guests ask for vegan, Jain, diabetic or allergy-free food. What should I say?
answer: Ask for needs at booking and agree what you can do. Say plainly if you cannot guarantee a nut-free or fully separate kitchen. Never guess about allergies, because they can be dangerous. Offer simple, safe alternatives.
actions: Ask about allergies and diet in your booking message.
Tell guests honestly what you can and cannot do.
Label dishes and keep allergen foods separate.
caution: For allergy and food safety rules, see food-safety guidance and your local food safety officer.
evidence: Good practice for village hosts; consistent with community-tourism principles in the bank sources, no single rule.

question_en: A guest in a wheelchair wants to come. Should I say yes?
answer: Ask what the guest needs and be honest about your space. If you can offer a ground-floor room and a wide door, say so. If not, say so kindly and suggest another host. Do not promise what you cannot give.
actions: Ask the guest to describe their needs.
Check steps, doors, bathroom and paths for access.
Say what you can and cannot offer, in writing.
caution: Do not attempt to lift or carry guests without training.
evidence: Good practice for village hosts; consistent with community-tourism principles in the bank sources, no single rule.

question_en: What should I tell guests before they arrive and at check-in?
answer: Tell them how to reach, the last stretch of road, what to carry, weather, food, toilet type, hot water, charging, network and house rules. Repeat the key points at check-in and show the room and the emergency contact.
actions: Send a pre-arrival message with route, what to bring and house rules.
At check-in, walk the guest through the room, toilet and water.
Share the host's phone number and the emergency contacts.
evidence: Good practice for village hosts; consistent with community-tourism principles in the bank sources, no single rule.

question_en: How do I write house rules that do not sound rude?
answer: Write rules as polite requests with a reason. For example, 'Please keep voices low after 10 pm because our children sleep.' Keep it to five to eight rules, in simple words, and share them before arrival and at check-in.
actions: List the five most important rules and the reason for each.
Write them as 'please' sentences.
Put them on a card in the room and in your pre-arrival message.
caution: Rules on legal matters, such as alcohol, must follow local law.
evidence: Good practice for village hosts; consistent with community-tourism principles in the bank sources, no single rule.

question_en: Guests ask about Western toilet, mosquito net, hot water, charging and power cuts. What should I say?
answer: Say clearly what you have: toilet type, whether hot water is solar, geyser or bucket, nets or repellents, charging points, internet and power cuts. Guests accept simple facilities when told in advance. Surprises cause complaints.
actions: List your basic facilities in a short paragraph.
State true limits: power cuts, limited hot water hours, weak signal.
Offer small fixes such as a torch, extension board or mosquito net.
evidence: Good practice for village hosts; consistent with community-tourism principles in the bank sources, no single rule.

question_en: Guests bring pets, or my family dog worries guests. What is the rule?
answer: Decide if you allow pets and say it before booking. Tell guests about your own dogs or livestock, and keep them away from guests who are afraid. Ask visitors to keep their pets leashed and away from kitchens and farm animals.
actions: State your pet policy in the booking message.
Tell guests about animals on the property at check-in.
Keep food areas free of animals.
caution: Rabies and bites are serious. Advise anyone bitten to see a doctor at once.
evidence: Good practice for village hosts; consistent with community-tourism principles in the bank sources, no single rule.

question_en: Guests want to drink or smoke at my homestay. What should I allow?
answer: Decide your own rule and write it. Many families prefer no smoking indoors and no alcohol in common areas. Alcohol laws differ by state, and some places are dry. Check your local rule before you allow or serve any.
actions: Check local alcohol law with the district excise office.
Write your rule in the house rules.
Say it kindly at check-in and ask again if rules are broken.
caution: Serving or selling alcohol may need a licence in many places. Do not do it without checking.
evidence: Good practice for village hosts; consistent with community-tourism principles in the bank sources, no single rule.

question_en: Guests play loud music at night and neighbours complain. What do I do?
answer: Set quiet hours and say them before booking. Speak to the group politely first, then firmly. Offer an outdoor corner or earlier time for music. If it continues, you may ask them to stop or leave.
actions: Write quiet hours in your rules.
Speak to the group's leader early and kindly.
Keep a note of what you said and when.
caution: If there is a threat or fight, call local police and move people to safety.
evidence: Good practice for village hosts; consistent with community-tourism principles in the bank sources, no single rule.

question_en: How do I keep my family kitchen and bedrooms private while guests are in the house?
answer: Mark which areas are for guests and which are for the family. Use a sign, a door or a curtain. Tell guests at check-in. Create a time when the family is off-duty and say it kindly.
actions: Mark guest and family areas with signs or doors.
Explain the boundary at check-in.
Keep fixed rest times for the family.
evidence: Good practice for village hosts; consistent with community-tourism principles in the bank sources, no single rule.

question_en: Guests wear very short clothes in the village. How do I tell them?
answer: Tell guests before arrival in a gentle way: 'In our village people dress modestly, especially near temples and homes. Please carry covered clothing.' Do this to all guests, not one person. Avoid shaming anyone.
actions: Add a dress note to the pre-arrival message.
Share the reason: respect for local customs.
Offer a shawl or dupatta at holy places if you can.
caution: Do not use harsh language.
evidence: UN Tourism Global Code of Ethics (read) says tourists must respect local traditions; method is practice.

question_en: Visitors take photos of villagers without asking. How do I stop it?
answer: Tell guests that people are not objects. Ask first, show the photo and respect a no. Put this in the house rules and orientation. Guides should remind guests before every visit.
actions: Add a photo rule to your orientation sheet.
Brief guests before every village walk.
Politely stop anyone who ignores the rule.
caution: Never photograph children, women at work or sacred events without permission.
evidence: Good practice for village hosts; consistent with community-tourism principles in the bank sources, no single rule.

question_en: Guests give sweets and pens to village children. Is this a problem?
answer: It can be. It encourages begging and can harm teeth and schooling. Ask guests not to give gifts directly. If they want to help, suggest giving to the school or a community fund through a trusted person.
actions: Tell guests not to hand out sweets or pens.
Name a school or village fund for donations.
Teach children and parents the plan too.
caution: Do not allow guests to take children alone.
evidence: Good practice for village hosts; consistent with community-tourism principles in the bank sources, no single rule.

question_en: How do I encourage guests to buy from local makers without being pushy?
answer: Show products with a name, price and maker's story. Allow guests to meet the maker. Do not push; say 'you are welcome to look'. Pay makers fairly and promptly and tell guests that buying directly helps them.
actions: Create a small display with maker names and prices.
Introduce guests to makers during visits.
Pay makers on time and keep a record.
caution: Do not sell items made with protected materials such as certain wood, skins or shells.
evidence: Good practice for village hosts; consistent with community-tourism principles in the bank sources, no single rule.

question_en: What steps should I follow from first enquiry to follow-up after the guest leaves?
answer: Think of six steps: enquiry, booking, arrival, stay, departure and follow-up. At each step, decide what you say, what you prepare and what you note. A simple flow helps new hosts stay calm and consistent.
actions: Write the six steps and one task for each.
Create one saved message for each step.
Review the flow after the first five guests.
evidence: Good practice for village hosts; consistent with community-tourism principles in the bank sources, no single rule.

question_en: What should I do at check-in and check-out?
answer: At check-in, welcome, show the room, explain water, toilet, power and rules, collect required details and share contacts. At check-out, check the room together, settle the bill with a receipt, thank the guest and ask for feedback.
actions: Walk the guest through the room and facilities at arrival.
Record guest details in your register as required locally.
Inspect the room, give a receipt and ask for feedback at departure.
caution: Registration rules for guest details differ. Ask your local police or tourism office.
evidence: General practice; Ministry of Tourism 2020 homestay recommendations (read, COVID-era) mention check-in details and linen change after check-out.

question_en: What must be checked in a room before guests arrive?
answer: Check that the room is clean, dry and free of insects, with fresh linen, working light, a lock, drinking water and a clean toilet. Smell the room and test the fan and plugs. Do this check yourself on the day.
actions: Clean, air and dry the room and change the linen.
Test lights, fan, plugs, lock and tap.
Leave drinking water, a torch and the house card in the room.
evidence: Good practice for village hosts; consistent with community-tourism principles in the bank sources, no single rule.

question_en: How often should I change bedsheets and towels?
answer: Change linen for every new guest. For long stays, change on a fixed day or when the guest asks. Wash in hot or soapy water and dry in sun. Never reuse sheets between guests without washing.
actions: Change sheets and towels after every guest.
Set a fixed linen-change day for long stays.
Dry in sun and store in a clean, dry cupboard.
caution: Ministry of Tourism 2020 homestay recommendations (COVID-era) said linen should be changed after every check-out.
evidence: Ministry of Tourism June 2020 operational recommendations for homestays (read, COVID-era, may be outdated); practice general.

question_en: What is a good bathroom standard for guests?
answer: A bathroom should be clean, odour-free, well lit, dry on the floor and have water, soap, toilet paper or a mug, a bin and a hook. Clean after every guest and again daily. Check for slippery floors.
actions: Clean and disinfect the toilet after every guest and daily.
Stock soap, water, bin and light.
Check floors, locks and drains for safety.
caution: Use cleaning chemicals as per the label and keep them away from children.
evidence: Good practice for village hosts; consistent with community-tourism principles in the bank sources, no single rule.

question_en: What is a good routine for welcome drink and breakfast?
answer: Offer a simple welcome drink on arrival, such as water, tea or a local drink. Agree breakfast time the evening before. Prepare in advance, serve hot food, and ask about diet and preferences. Keep it simple and consistent.
actions: Offer a welcome drink and ask about food needs.
Confirm breakfast time the night before.
Serve in clean plates and keep the area tidy.
caution: Follow food hygiene rules and ask the local food safety officer.
evidence: Good practice for village hosts; consistent with community-tourism principles in the bank sources, no single rule.

question_en: Guests arrive at midnight without telling me. What do I do?
answer: Ask guests to tell you their arrival time. Keep your phone on. Agree a latest arrival time and what you will do after it. Keep a simple cold meal or tea and a key arrangement so you are not woken at all hours.
actions: Ask guests for expected arrival time at booking.
Share a phone number and a latest check-in time.
Keep a snack and a spare key plan ready.
caution: If the guest is lost on a rural road at night, send help only in a safe way and call a known person.
evidence: Good practice for village hosts; consistent with community-tourism principles in the bank sources, no single rule.

question_en: A guest is angry about the room. How do I handle a complaint?
answer: Listen without interrupting, say sorry that the guest is upset, and ask what would help. Fix what you can on the spot and offer a small, fair remedy if justified. Note the issue and fix its cause.
actions: Listen calmly and repeat the problem back.
Offer a clear fix or alternative.
Write down the complaint and the action.
caution: If the complaint involves safety or harassment, treat it as serious and contact authorities as needed.
evidence: Good practice for village hosts; consistent with community-tourism principles in the bank sources, no single rule.

question_en: A guest lost something, or broke an item. What is the fair way?
answer: For lost items, record them, keep them safely and tell the guest. For damage, check and agree on cost fairly, and show proof. Say your damage policy in the house rules so there is no surprise.
actions: Keep a lost-and-found notebook.
Take photos of damage and agree repair cost kindly.
State the damage rule in the house card.
caution: Do not accuse. Do not keep a guest's belongings as pressure.
evidence: Good practice for village hosts; consistent with community-tourism principles in the bank sources, no single rule.

question_en: A guest did not come, or I accidentally booked the room twice. What now?
answer: For a no-show, call and message, wait a reasonable time and then follow your stated policy. For an overbooking, tell the guests immediately, apologise, and find a similar nearby home and cover any extra cost. Use a shared calendar to avoid repeats.
actions: Keep one calendar for all bookings.
Contact guests as soon as you notice a problem.
Offer an alternative and cover reasonable costs.
evidence: Good practice for village hosts; consistent with community-tourism principles in the bank sources, no single rule.

question_en: Guests bargain hard even for a fixed price. How do I respond?
answer: Say the price is fixed and explain what it covers. If you offer a discount, give it for a clear reason like a longer stay and apply it fairly. Do not reduce the pay of workers to keep the price low.
actions: Publish fixed prices and discount rules.
Say your line kindly and calmly.
Offer a smaller package if the budget is lower.
evidence: Good practice for village hosts; consistent with community-tourism principles in the bank sources, no single rule.

question_en: A guest ignores my rules. What can I do?
answer: Remind them calmly in private. Refer to the house card. If it continues, give a clear warning and a deadline. If safety or others' comfort is at risk, you may ask them to leave according to your policy. Keep notes.
actions: Speak in private and politely first.
Give a clear warning and what will happen next.
Record each step in a notebook.
caution: If there is violence, theft or harassment, call local police.
evidence: Good practice for village hosts; consistent with community-tourism principles in the bank sources, no single rule.

question_en: What should be on my emergency contact sheet?
answer: Make one page with host phone numbers, nearest health centre and hospital, local doctor, police station, fire, ambulance, vehicle driver, village head and a family member. Check the numbers every season. Keep copies in the kitchen, the guest room and the phone.
actions: List contacts and write the distance to each.
Check that each number works every season.
Share the sheet with guests and family.
caution: Verify national and state emergency numbers on official sources before printing.
evidence: Good practice for village hosts; consistent with community-tourism principles in the bank sources, no single rule.

question_en: What daily and weekly routines keep a homestay running well?
answer: Every day: clean rooms and toilets, check water, stock supplies, note bookings. Every week: wash linen, check beds, plugs, nets and drains, count supplies and update the notebook. Short checks prevent big problems.
actions: Write a daily and a weekly list and put it on the wall.
Share tasks among family members.
Tick each task so you can see what is missing.
evidence: Good practice for village hosts; consistent with community-tourism principles in the bank sources, no single rule.

question_en: What records should I keep? I am not good with paperwork.
answer: Keep two simple notebooks. One is the guest register with date, name, number of guests, nights and payment. The other is an income and expense book with date, item and amount. Write daily. Add a page for complaints and feedback.
actions: Buy two notebooks and rule columns as above.
Write every payment and expense the same day.
Total the pages once a month.
caution: Rules on guest registers and accounts differ. Ask your local police or an accountant.
evidence: Good practice for village hosts; consistent with community-tourism principles in the bank sources, no single rule.

question_en: What should I repair or prepare before each season?
answer: Before monsoon, check roofs, drains, walls and wiring. Before summer, check fans, water storage and shade. Before winter, check blankets, heating and ventilation. Repair in the slow months, not when guests are in the house.
actions: Make a seasonal checklist for roof, water, power and bedding.
Repair in slow months.
Test every plug, tap and lock before the season starts.
caution: Wiring, gas and structure need a qualified person.
evidence: Good practice for village hosts; consistent with community-tourism principles in the bank sources, no single rule.

question_en: Mosquitoes and insects are a problem for guests. What can I do safely?
answer: Remove standing water around the house, keep windows screened, offer mosquito nets, and keep food covered. Use cleaning and sealing first. Use pesticides only as directed on the label, never near food, and keep them away from children.
actions: Empty water containers and clear drains every week.
Fit nets or screens and offer bed nets.
Store food covered and waste in closed bins.
caution: Do not use unlabelled or banned pesticides. In areas with mosquito-borne disease, follow health department advice.
evidence: Good practice for village hosts; consistent with community-tourism principles in the bank sources, no single rule.

question_en: Everyone in my family has a different idea. How do we divide the work of hosting?
answer: Sit together and list tasks: welcome, cooking, cleaning, laundry, accounts, guiding and bookings. Ask each person what they like and can do. Share the money and the load fairly and write it down. Review every season.
actions: List tasks on one page and ask each person to choose.
Agree how income is shared and record it.
Review roles every season.
evidence: Good practice for village hosts; consistent with community-tourism principles in the bank sources, no single rule.

question_en: Will hosting affect my children's studies?
answer: It can if children are made to work for guests. Protect school hours and study time. Let children join only in light, safe, voluntary ways, such as greeting guests, outside school hours. Children should not do heavy work or serve alone.
actions: Fix school and study hours as no-guest time.
Keep children's role light and voluntary.
Never leave children alone with guests.
caution: Child labour laws apply. Do not employ children in your business.
evidence: Good practice for village hosts; consistent with community-tourism principles in the bank sources, no single rule.

question_en: Women do most of the work in hosting. How can we make it fair?
answer: Tourism should not simply add to women's unpaid work. Pay women for their work, share chores, and let women decide what they host. Plan breaks, and keep women's decisions and income in their own hands.
actions: Count the hours women spend and write them down.
Share tasks with men and youth in the household.
Pay women directly for their work.
evidence: UN Tourism Global Code of Ethics (read) calls for equitable sharing of benefits; method is practice.

question_en: I am tired all the time with guests. How do I avoid burnout?
answer: Limit the number of guests and the number of days per month. Keep rest days, share work and raise prices if you are always full. Ask for help early. Tourism should improve life, not exhaust it.
actions: Set a maximum number of guest nights per month.
Fix weekly rest days with no guests.
Raise price or reduce group size if overworked.
evidence: Good practice for village hosts; consistent with community-tourism principles in the bank sources, no single rule.

question_en: How can I say no to a guest politely?
answer: Say it kindly and give a reason or an alternative. For example, 'We cannot do that, but we can offer this.' Keep your tone calm. You are the host and you may protect your family and your culture.
actions: Prepare two polite sentences for common requests.
Offer an alternative where possible.
Stay firm if the request is unsafe or against your values.
evidence: Good practice for village hosts; consistent with community-tourism principles in the bank sources, no single rule.

question_en: How do I stay safe with strangers in my home?
answer: Keep family bedrooms and valuables away from guest areas, lock them, and keep a phone nearby. Collect guest details and keep emergency numbers ready. Tell a neighbour when large groups come. Trust your instinct and ask unsafe guests to leave.
actions: Lock family rooms and valuables.
Tell a neighbour or relative about large bookings.
Keep emergency numbers handy.
caution: If you feel threatened, call local police.
evidence: Good practice for village hosts; consistent with community-tourism principles in the bank sources, no single rule.

question_en: Neighbours are jealous or unhappy about my guests. What can I do?
answer: Talk with neighbours early. Share the benefits: buy their produce, hire their skills, or send guests to their shop or craft. Explain your quiet hours. Invite their ideas. Tourism works better when many families gain.
actions: Visit neighbours and explain your plan.
Buy or refer guests to neighbours' goods and services.
Fix problems quickly when noise or crowds disturb them.
evidence: Good practice for village hosts; consistent with community-tourism principles in the bank sources, no single rule.

question_en: Our village wants rules for visitors. How do we write a code of conduct?
answer: Hold a village meeting and ask what visitors should and should not do. Keep rules short and positive, such as asking before photos, modest dress, no litter and quiet hours. Print them in local language and English, and display them at a visitor point.
actions: Call a meeting with women, youth and elders.
Write five to eight simple rules in local language.
Display them and give them to every guest.
caution: Rules must follow the law and gram panchayat decisions.
evidence: Good practice for village hosts; consistent with community-tourism principles in the bank sources, no single rule.

question_en: Can we make one place where visitors first arrive and get information?
answer: Yes. A shaded spot with a map, the code of conduct, activity list with fair rates, toilets, drinking water and a village host can work. Visitors can be guided to homes in turns. It protects privacy and spreads income.
actions: Choose a safe, shaded place near the entry.
Display map, rates, rules and emergency contacts.
Train two or three local hosts to run it.
evidence: Good practice for village hosts; consistent with community-tourism principles in the bank sources, no single rule.

question_en: Some homes get all the guests and others none. How can we share fairly?
answer: Make a simple rotation list of ready homes and assign guests in turn, keeping family choice and guest needs in mind. Set minimum standards a home must meet to join. Review the list every season.
actions: List homes that meet the minimum standard.
Assign guests in turn and write it in a shared register.
Review the rotation every season.
evidence: Good practice for village hosts; consistent with community-tourism principles in the bank sources, no single rule.

question_en: How can all hosts track bookings so we do not double book?
answer: Use one shared booking calendar, on paper at the visitor point or on a shared phone sheet kept by a trusted person. Update it on every booking and cancellation. Mark festival days and rest days.
actions: Choose one keeper for the shared calendar.
Update after every booking or change.
Mark festival and rest days.
caution: Protect guests' personal details. Share only dates and room counts.
evidence: Good practice for village hosts; consistent with community-tourism principles in the bank sources, no single rule.

question_en: How do we make sure every home in the village has similar cleanliness and fair prices?
answer: Agree a short checklist for room, toilet, water, food and safety, and a price range. Visit each other's homes in pairs to help, not to blame. Offer training. Keep prices fair, but check local rules about price agreements.
actions: Write a one-page checklist agreed by all hosts.
Do peer visits and share tips.
Hold a short training each season.
caution: Group pricing agreements may have legal limits. Ask a legal adviser.
evidence: Good practice for village hosts; consistent with community-tourism principles in the bank sources, no single rule.

question_en: Villagers complain about noise, crowding and litter from tourists. What should we do?
answer: Listen to the complaints in a village meeting and write them down. Choose quick fixes: limits on groups, quiet hours, waste bins, route changes and a contact person. Report back what was done. If problems continue, slow tourism down.
actions: Hold a meeting and record complaints.
Agree three actions and a person for each.
Report progress at the next meeting.
evidence: Good practice for village hosts; consistent with community-tourism principles in the bank sources, no single rule.

question_en: How many visitors can our village handle? What about festival days?
answer: There is no single number. Look at water, waste, parking, toilets, noise and how people feel. Set a daily limit that the village agrees on and review it. On festival days, limit visitors or ask guests to join only as invited, because the festival belongs to the community.
actions: List the things that become crowded first, such as water or parking.
Agree a trial daily limit and test it.
Decide festival-day rules in advance and tell guests.
evidence: Good practice for village hosts; consistent with community-tourism principles in the bank sources, no single rule.

question_en: Who decides what part of our culture we show to visitors?
answer: The community decides, not the host alone or an outsider. Hold open meetings with women, elders, youth and the groups concerned. List what may be shared, what may be shared with conditions, and what is private or sacred. Record the decision and review it.
actions: Hold an open meeting and list items in three groups: share, share with conditions, do not share.
Record who agreed and when.
Review the list each year.
caution: Sacred or private rituals, and the knowledge of specific families, need their own permission.
evidence: UN Tourism Global Code of Ethics (read) says tourism should respect culture and local participation; method is practice.

question_en: How do I run a village meeting so that everyone, including women and youth, speaks?
answer: Tell people the date, time and topic early. Meet at a time women can attend. Use small groups and let everyone speak in turn. Write decisions on a chart in local language and read them out. Avoid long speeches.
actions: Fix a time and place that suits women and elders.
Use small groups and one question at a time.
Write and read out the decisions before closing.
evidence: Good practice for village hosts; consistent with community-tourism principles in the bank sources, no single rule.

question_en: Two hosts fight over guests and money. How do we settle it?
answer: Agree a simple process beforehand: listen to both sides separately, then together, with two neutral elders or leaders. Record the decision. If it is serious, refer it to the gram panchayat or the appropriate authority.
actions: Write a three-step conflict process.
Choose two neutral people who both sides respect.
Record agreements and review them.
caution: Legal or criminal matters must go to the proper authority.
evidence: Good practice for village hosts; consistent with community-tourism principles in the bank sources, no single rule.

question_en: How can our youth take part in tourism without leaving the village?
answer: Youth can become guides, drivers, photographers, social media helpers, storytellers and booking coordinators. Train and pay them fairly. Pair them with elders so they learn the culture properly. Let them take responsibility.
actions: Ask youth which roles they want.
Offer small training and a mentor.
Pay youth fairly and give them real tasks.
evidence: Good practice for village hosts; consistent with community-tourism principles in the bank sources, no single rule.

question_en: How do we keep tourism money open and trusted in the village?
answer: Keep a simple ledger of all money in and out, with receipts. Two people should hold the cash. Read the totals out at a village meeting every few months. Keep the book open for anyone to see.
actions: Use a bound notebook with dated entries.
Have two people check cash and the book.
Read the totals publicly each quarter.
caution: Money rules apply. Ask an accountant for the correct way to hold community funds.
evidence: Good practice for village hosts; consistent with community-tourism principles in the bank sources, no single rule.

question_en: What should I ask guests for feedback? Long forms are not read.
answer: Ask four or five short questions: What did you enjoy most? What can we improve? Was the price fair for what you got? Did you feel safe and respected? Would you recommend us? Use a paper card or a phone message.
actions: Write five questions on a card.
Ask at departure and send a message later.
Write each answer in a notebook.
evidence: Good practice for village hosts; consistent with community-tourism principles in the bank sources, no single rule.

question_en: How do I test an experience before selling it?
answer: Invite friendly guests or neighbours for a trial at no or low cost. Run it as a real experience with real timing. Ask them for honest feedback, note what went wrong and fix it. Repeat until it runs smoothly, then sell.
actions: Run a trial with friends and family first.
Time each step and note problems.
Fix and test again before selling.
caution: Do not skip safety checks during the trial.
evidence: Good practice for village hosts; consistent with community-tourism principles in the bank sources, no single rule.

question_en: How can I track how my tourism is doing without a computer?
answer: Once a month write five numbers: guests, guest nights, income, expenses and complaints or praise. Add one line on what you learned. Compare with the previous month and season. This tells you if the work is worth it.
actions: Draw a table with the five columns.
Fill it at month end.
Discuss the page with your family.
evidence: Good practice for village hosts; consistent with community-tourism principles in the bank sources, no single rule.

question_en: Something went wrong with a group. How do we learn without blaming?
answer: Sit together the next day. Ask what happened, why, and what we will change. Do not blame persons; fix the process. Write the change and share it. Mistakes shared early become lessons.
actions: Hold a short review after any problem.
Write one change and who will do it.
Share the lesson with other hosts.
evidence: Good practice for village hosts; consistent with community-tourism principles in the bank sources, no single rule.

question_en: When should I add rooms or more activities, and when should I stop?
answer: Expand only if you are full for several seasons, guests are happy and your family is not tired. Grow slowly, one step at a time. Stop or pause if the village is unhappy, the quality falls, or the work harms family life or the environment.
actions: Check occupancy, quality and family energy before growing.
Grow one thing at a time.
Pause when community or family says stop.
caution: Do not take large loans without a clear plan. Ask a bank or finance adviser.
evidence: Good practice for village hosts; consistent with community-tourism principles in the bank sources, no single rule.

question_en: Our village is becoming popular on social media. How do we avoid becoming too crowded?
answer: Plan before the crowd arrives. Set group size and daily limits, spread guests across homes and days, and ask for advance booking. Keep local life first. Do not advertise places that cannot handle crowds.
actions: Set group size and daily limits.
Ask for advance booking at busy times.
Review the effects on village life each season.
evidence: Good practice for village hosts; consistent with community-tourism principles in the bank sources, no single rule.

question_en: What if tourists suddenly stop coming because of weather, road closure or news?
answer: Do not rely on tourism alone. Keep farming, crafts and other work, and save a part of the good-season income. When bookings drop, use the time for training and repairs, talk to past guests, and keep your costs low.
actions: Keep another source of income.
Save a small reserve from peak season.
Use quiet time to fix and learn.
caution: Do not borrow heavily for tourism.
evidence: Good practice for village hosts; consistent with community-tourism principles in the bank sources, no single rule.
